snapshots.name: Publius
snapshots.subtitle: The shared pseudonym of three writers
snapshots.body: The single name under which all 85 essays appeared, concealing three actual authors — Alexander Hamilton, James Madison, and John Jay — writing to persuade New York to ratify the proposed Constitution. Each essay speaks in one unified voice regardless of which of the three actually wrote it, and this served edition does not credit essays by author in the body text.

snapshots.name: Faction
snapshots.subtitle: No. 10's central problem
snapshots.body: Defined in No. 10 as a number of citizens, whether a minority or a majority, united by some common impulse of passion or interest adverse to the rights of others or the permanent interests of the community — the danger Publius argues an extended republic is uniquely suited to control.

snapshots.name: Ambition Must Counteract Ambition
snapshots.subtitle: No. 51's design principle
snapshots.body: The structural argument of No. 51: since no government of angels is available, the Constitution's separated departments must each be given the constitutional means and personal motives to resist encroachment by the others, so that ambition is made to counteract ambition.

snapshots.name: The Union
snapshots.subtitle: The good the whole work defends
snapshots.body: The confederated whole whose preservation the essays repeatedly argue is essential to safety, commerce, and liberty alike — introduced in the opening essay as involving nothing less than the existence of the Union and the fate of the American experiment.

snapshots.name: Republican Government
snapshots.subtitle: What makes a government 'strictly republican'
snapshots.body: The form of government No. 39 defines and defends: one that derives all its powers, directly or indirectly, from the great body of the people, and is administered by persons holding their offices during good behavior or for a limited period — the form Publius insists the proposed Constitution is.

snapshots.name: The Judiciary, "Least Dangerous" Branch
snapshots.subtitle: No. 78's famous defense
snapshots.body: The department No. 78 argues has neither force nor will but merely judgment, and must depend on the other branches even for the efficacy of its judgments — the branch Publius calls, of the three, always the least dangerous to the political rights established by the Constitution.

snapshots.name: A Vigorous Executive
snapshots.subtitle: No. 70's defense of a single president
snapshots.body: The case No. 70 makes against the idea that a strong executive is incompatible with republican government: energy in the executive, Publius argues, is a leading characteristic of good government, and a feeble execution is only another name for bad execution.

snapshots.name: The Accumulation of All Powers
snapshots.subtitle: "The very definition of tyranny"
snapshots.body: No. 47's warning, echoing Montesquieu: the accumulation of legislative, executive, and judicial power in the same hands, whether one, a few, or many, and whether inherited, self-appointed, or elective, may justly be called the very definition of tyranny.
